title: What is known about 1RB1RA_0RC1RC_1LD0LF_0LE1LE_1RA0LB_---0LC
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1RA_0RC1RC_1LD0LF_0LE1LE_1RA0LB_---0LC.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape. Its run is a sequence of epochs, each a Collatz-like countdown; an epoch ends either in a halt or in a new, vastly longer epoch. The bbchallenge community lists it as probviously halting: with fair-coin parities every epoch halts with probability 1/3.
verdict: The question is open. In configurations X(n, m) = C>0 0^n 1^m 0 1 the machine sends n to about 3n/2 and m down by 1 or 2 according to n mod 4. When m runs out it halts or starts a new epoch with m ≈ 3n/2.

Where the run is (computed exactly). Epochs start with m = 5, 57, 210,273,201. The third epoch lasts 140,180,848 macro steps (the number reaches 82 million bits) and ends in a new epoch, whose countdown has about 24,684,623 decimal digits. Its end is out of reach of any computation. Heuristically each epoch halts with probability 1/3, so the machine halts with probability 1, after a number of steps with tens of millions of digits in its exponent.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 36,156 cells have been visited and 24,110 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: The macro rules
claims.text: For X(n, m) = 0^∞ C>0 0^n 1^m 0 1 0^∞ with n ≥ 2 even: for m ≥ 2, n ≡ 0 (mod 4) goes to X(3n/2 + 4, m − 1) and n ≡ 2 to X((3n + 10)/2, m − 2); for m = 1, n ≡ 0 gives X(3n/2 + 4, 0) and n ≡ 2 a new epoch X(4, 3n/2 + 6); for m = 0, n ≡ 0 gives X(4, 3n/2 + 5) and n ≡ 2 halts. Checked against direct simulation for every even 2 ≤ n < 60 and m < 12. Inside a step the head fills the run of 0s with 1s from the left, two cells per round trip while the tape grows by one at the left; then a 1 is taken off the countdown block.

claims.title: The first three epochs, exactly
claims.text: From blank tape the run reaches X(4, 5) after 50 steps; epochs start with m = 5, 57 (step 2,619) and 210,273,201. The third epoch was run exactly with a divide-and-conquer parity iteration (the parities of t steps of y ↦ ⌈3y/2⌉ depend only on y mod 2<sup>t</sup>; blocks are combined with powers of 3, GMP through gmpy2): it ends after 140,180,848 macro steps at m = 1 with n ≡ 2 (mod 4), so a fourth epoch starts with m = 3n/2 + 6, a number of 82,000,544 bits (about 24,684,623 digits; m mod 2<sup>64</sup> = 15369781771884450229). Two runs with different block sizes agree; the fast iteration agrees with plain big-integer iteration on epochs with m up to 10<sup>5</sup>.

claims.title: Halts with probability 1, but not soon
claims.text: With y = n/2 + 4 the rule is y ↦ ⌈3y/2⌉, with m −1 for y even and −2 for y odd. With fair-coin parities the countdown lands on m = 1 with probability 2/3 and on 0 with probability 1/3; m = 1 continues to 0 or starts a new epoch, and m = 0 halts or starts a new epoch, each with probability 1/2. So an epoch halts with probability 1/3 and the machine halts with probability 1, the community's reading. The fourth epoch alone lasts about 10<sup>24,684,623</sup> macro steps.

claims.title: How does the fourth epoch end?
claims.text: It needs the parities of about 1.6 · 10<sup>24,684,622</sup> iterates of ⌈3y/2⌉ from y = 6: no method computes them.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows whether it halts, but almost everyone expects it to — eventually. This machine plays rounds of a game: a number grows by a factor 3/2 while a countdown ticks down by 1 or 2, depending on the number's last binary digits. When the countdown runs out, the machine either halts or starts a new round with a countdown about 3/2 times the number. We computed the third round exactly — 140 million steps of the game. It does not halt: it starts a fourth round whose countdown has almost 25 million digits.

facts.text: Countdowns of the first three epochs, computed exactly.
The fourth epoch's countdown: out of reach.
Chance an epoch ends in a halt with fair-coin parities.

sections.heading: Rounds of a 3/2 game
html: Over and over, the head stands at the left end of the tape in state C, looking at a run of 0s, then a block of 1s, then 0 1:

<svg viewBox="0 0 640 110" role="img" aria-label="the tape at a macro configuration" style="width:100%;max-width:640px;height:auto;font:12px var(--mono)">
<polygon points="8,40 20,57 8,74" fill="var(--head)"/><text x="4" y="92" fill="var(--head)">C</text>
<rect x="24" y="40" width="330" height="34" fill="var(--cell0)" stroke="var(--line-strong)"/><text x="189" y="62" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--fg)">0^n — the number</text>
<rect x="358" y="40" width="200" height="34" fill="var(--accent-soft)" stroke="var(--accent)"/><text x="458" y="62" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--fg)">1^m — the countdown</text>
<rect x="562" y="40" width="20" height="34" fill="var(--cell0)" stroke="var(--line-strong)"/><rect x="586" y="40" width="20" height="34" fill="var(--sunk)" stroke="var(--line-strong)"/><text x="596" y="62" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--fg)">1</text>
<text x="189" y="28" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--fg2)">n → about 3n/2 per step</text><text x="458" y="28" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--fg2)">m → m−1 or m−2</text></svg>

From there the head sweeps back and forth, filling the 0s with 1s two at a time from the left while the tape grows by one cell at the left each round trip, and then takes one or two 1s off the countdown. The net effect: n becomes 3n/2 + 4 and the countdown loses 1 if n is a multiple of 4; n becomes (3n + 10)/2 and the countdown loses 2 otherwise. With y = n/2 + 4 the number simply goes y ↦ ⌈3y/2⌉.

When the countdown is used up the round ends: with one parity the machine halts, with the other it starts a new round with n = 4 and a countdown of about 3n/2. Since n has grown by a factor 3/2 per step, every round's countdown is exponentially longer than the last.

From blank tape the rounds start with countdowns 5, 57 and 210,273,201. We played the third round exactly: 140,180,848 steps of the game, with the number growing to 82 million binary digits. The trick is that the parities of the next t steps depend only on the last t binary digits of y, so long stretches can be computed by divide and conquer (35 seconds instead of years). The round did not halt: it started a fourth round whose countdown has about 24,684,623 decimal digits. That round can never be played out.

If the parities behave like fair coins, each round halts with probability 1/3, so the machine should halt eventually — that is what probviously halting means — but only after a number of steps far too large to write down, and nobody can prove it.

explainer.title: A countdown that resets into a bigger one

summary: Epochs of y ↦ ⌈3y/2⌉ with a countdown m (−1 even, −2 odd); an epoch ends in a halt or a new epoch with m ≈ 3y. Computed exactly: epochs start at m = 5, 57, 210,273,201 and then a 24.7-million-digit m; probviously halting, but open.
